meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (informal)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What did you lose in my kitchen?

examples.trans: Misha, go to your own office.

examples.text: Ты чем думал, когда пожар в номере устроил?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'fire' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Here is a new 'Chef to the Room' order.

meanings.en: to arrange, organize, set up an event or scheme
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'строить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to arrange, organize, set up', paired with 'устраивать'.

examples.text: Ты чем думал, когда пожар в номере устроил?
examples.trans: What were you thinking when you started a fire in the room?

examples.text: Я всё устрою на высшем уровне.
examples.trans: I will arrange everything at the highest level.
They organized a party for friends.

examples.trans: I want him to leave.

So should I leave?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to me', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Our restaurant is located right here.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'sauce' (ultimately from Latin 'salsa', salted seasoning).

examples.trans: In France this sauce is considered one of the foundational ones.
It is one of the main sauces.
One must not abandon the preparation of our sauce.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'нимать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to take off the heat', paired with 'снять'.

examples.trans: Back off, I need to take the sauce off the heat.

meanings.en: must, need to, it is necessary

examples.trans: I hope we will avoid such conversations.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what, that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And where is your head chef right now?
Where is our chef right now, though?
What is happening over there right now?

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'делать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'make, cause'.

examples.trans: What have you just done?!

examples.text: Что, я зря пришла? Я надела костюм зайки!
examples.trans: What, did I come for nothing? I put on a bunny costume!

meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'it seems', paired with 'показаться'.

examples.text: Я должен рассказать Кате или нет?
examples.trans: Should I tell Katya or not?

examples.text: Катя, мне надо тебе кое-что сказать.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('secret, undercover').

examples.trans: Who is this secret guest?

examples.text: Тайный гость будет сегодня или завтра.
examples.trans: The secret guest will be here today or tomorrow.

examples.text: Мы должны встретить тайного гостя достойно.
examples.trans: We must welcome the secret guest properly.

meanings.note: Abstract feminine noun formed with the Slavic suffix '-ость' ('-ness, -ity') from the corresponding adjective. Common masculine noun meaning 'guest' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Гости ресторана — это не только посетители.
examples.trans: Restaurant guests are not just casual visitors.

Who is this secret guest?
